title: Can pulmonary sarcoidosis trigger a progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy? Considerations from a case series and a review of literature
case_prompt:
A 54-year-old woman presented with fatigue, bilateral visual impairment, vertigo, and gait instability. Neurological examination revealed left hemianopia, dysarthria, right hemiparesis (upper limb 4/5, lower limb 2/5), a positive Babinski sign, gait ataxia, attention deficit, and memory disturbance. Her history included arterial hypertension, chronic hepatitis B, and pulmonary sarcoidosis diagnosed six years earlier by mediastinal lymph node biopsy and consistent chest imaging without immunosuppressive treatment.  
Brain MRI (3.0 Tesla) showed diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintense white-matter lesions in the left frontal, right parietal, and both occipital lobes without mass effect or contrast enhancement; lesions were partially hypointense on T1-weighted scans.  
Tests for ANA, ENA, ANCA, and cardiolipin antibodies were unremarkable. CSF analysis revealed normal cell count, protein, glucose, and lactate but elevated albumin and IgG; oligoclonal bands were absent. Serologic and CSF studies for Lyme disease and common viral infections were negative; HIV testing was negative. Serum ACE level was elevated at 86.9 U/L (normal 18–55).  
Chest CT showed upper-lobe atelectasis and fibrosis with nodular lesions and hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy typical for sarcoidosis. FDG-PET demonstrated increased tracer uptake in large vessels, interpreted as vasculitis involvement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Primary central nervous system vasculitis was initially considered because of diffuse white-matter lesions and FDG-PET findings — “At first, these findings were felt to be suggestive of vasculitis.”  
2. Negative autoantibody panel made systemic vasculitis less likely — “testing for autoantibodies (ANA, ENA, ANCA, and cardiolipin-antibodies) … yielded unremarkable findings.”  
3. Neurosarcoidosis was suspected due to history of sarcoidosis and elevated ACE level, but brain biopsy showed no granulomas — “Histology revealed (peri)vascular inflammation, but showed no evidence for granulomas or polynuclear giant cells which would have been indicative of neurosarcoidosis.”  
4. Disease progression under immunosuppression and MRI lesion evolution raised PML suspicion — “The imaging characteristics and the lesion evolution finally led to considering the differential diagnosis of PML.”  
5. Detection of high JC virus DNA in CSF and urine and SV40 immunohistochemistry confirmed PML — “JCV testing … yielded 4.6 million copies in urine and 150 copies/mL in the CSF. An immunohistochemical reaction with the SV40/JC antibody was also seen in the brain tissue specimen.”
